pages.body:
Every day, the world burns millions of tonnes of coal, oil and gas to generate electricity and power vehicles. These fuels took hundreds of millions of years to form underground. But we are using them up in a few hundred years. And burning them releases gases that are warming the planet.

- Where does the electricity in your community come from? Is it renewable or non-renewable?
- What would happen to Ghana's energy supply if all its oil and gas ran out?
- Have you seen any solar panels or other renewable energy devices in your community?

> **DEFINITION** **Sustainable energy:** energy from sources that are naturally replenished and will not run out, and whose use does not cause lasting harm to the environment. **Renewable energy:** energy from sources that are continuously replenished by natural processes, such as sunlight, wind and flowing water. **Non-renewable energy:** energy from sources that formed over millions of years and cannot be replaced once used, such as coal, oil and natural gas. **Green economy:** an economy that aims for growth and development while reducing pollution, greenhouse gas emissions and environmental risks.

pages.title: What is a green economy?
pages.body: A green economy creates jobs and wealth while protecting the environment. It moves away from activities that damage the climate and ecosystems, and instead invests in clean energy, sustainable agriculture, green building and efficient transport. Ghana's government has included green economy principles in its national development plans.

| **Green economy sector** | **What it means for Ghana** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Clean energy | Expanding solar, wind and hydroelectric power instead of coal and diesel | Solar street lights; rooftop solar panels; rural solar mini-grids |
| Sustainable agriculture | Farming methods that protect soil, water and biodiversity while feeding the population | Organic farming; agroforestry; biogas from farm waste |
| Green buildings | Buildings designed to use less energy and water | Schools and homes with solar panels; energy-efficient lighting; proper insulation |
| Sustainable transport | Reducing emissions from vehicles | Electric motorcycles (e-bikes); fuel-efficient buses; cycling infrastructure in cities |
| Waste and recycling | Converting waste to energy or reusable materials | Biogas from organic waste; plastic recycling; composting |

> **Lesson 1 Assessment**

pages.body:
Ghana's farmers in the north are seeing rains arrive later each year. Fishing communities on the coast notice the sea rising and flooding their homes. Droughts are becoming longer and more severe. Forest fires are more common. All of these changes are connected to one global process that scientists have been warning about for decades.

- Have you noticed any changes in the weather or seasons in Ghana in your lifetime? What have you observed?
- Have you heard of the greenhouse effect or global warming? What do you know about it?
- Why do you think the actions of people far away in other countries can affect the climate in Ghana?

pages.title: What is the greenhouse effect?
pages.body:
The Earth's atmosphere acts like a giant greenhouse. The Sun sends energy to the Earth as short-wave radiation (sunlight). The Earth's surface absorbs this energy and releases it back as long-wave infrared radiation (heat). Certain gases in the atmosphere, called greenhouse gases, trap some of this outgoing heat and prevent it from escaping into space. This is the greenhouse effect.

The greenhouse effect is a natural process — without it, the Earth would be about 33 degrees Celsius colder and unable to support life. The problem occurs when human activities produce extra greenhouse gases, intensifying the greenhouse effect and trapping more heat than normal. This causes global warming.

[[img:iwr9t5i61]]

> **DEFINITION** **Greenhouse effect:** the process by which greenhouse gases in the atmosphere trap heat from the Sun, warming the Earth's surface. **Greenhouse gases (GHGs):** gases in the atmosphere that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, trapping heat. Main ones: carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O) and water vapour. **Global warming:** the long-term increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface, caused by the enhanced greenhouse effect from human activities. **Climate change:** the long-term shift in global weather patterns and temperatures caused by global warming. It includes changes in rainfall, sea levels, storm frequency and ecosystem disruption.

pages.title: Effects of climate change on Ghana and the world
pages.body:
| **Effect** | **How it affects Ghana specifically** |
|---|---|
| Rising temperatures | Higher average temperatures reduce crop yields, increase heat stress for workers and animals, and make malaria mosquitoes active in more areas. |
| Changes in rainfall patterns | Rainfall becomes less predictable: drought in the north reduces food production; heavier rainfall in the south causes flooding of coastal cities like Accra. |
| Sea level rise | Ghana's low-lying coastal communities — including parts of Accra, Tema and fishing villages — are at risk of flooding and erosion as sea levels rise. |
| Loss of biodiversity | Many plants and animals cannot adapt fast enough to rapidly changing conditions and face extinction. Forest ecosystems are disrupted. |
| Reduced water in rivers and dams | Lower rainfall and higher evaporation reduce water levels in Lake Volta and other water bodies, affecting hydroelectric power generation and drinking water supply. |
| More frequent extreme weather | Floods, droughts and storms are becoming more frequent and more severe, causing deaths, displacement of people and destruction of infrastructure. |
| Food insecurity | Changing seasons confuse farmers. Late rains and drought reduce maize, yam and cocoa yields. Higher food prices affect poor communities most. |

pages.title: How to minimise the greenhouse effect
pages.body:
**What individuals and communities can do**
- Switch from firewood and charcoal to biogas or LPG for cooking to reduce CO₂ and deforestation.
- Use energy-efficient LED lighting instead of incandescent bulbs.
- Plant trees (reforestation) to absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere.
- Reduce, reuse and recycle waste to reduce emissions from landfills.
- Use public transport, walk or cycle instead of private vehicles where possible.
- Educate family and community members about climate change and energy choices.

**What governments and industries must do**
- Invest in renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric) to replace fossil fuel power stations.
- Enforce laws against illegal burning of forest (bush fires) and galamsey (which destroys vegetation).
- Support climate-smart agriculture: drought-resistant crop varieties, irrigation, agroforestry.
- Sign and implement international climate agreements (e.g. the Paris Agreement, which Ghana has signed).
- Tax carbon-intensive industries and use the revenue to fund clean energy projects.
- Invest in coastal defences to protect communities from sea level rise.

> **Did you know?** Ghana signed the Paris Agreement on Climate Change in 2016, committing to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions and transition to cleaner energy. Ghana's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets include expanding renewable energy, reducing deforestation and promoting sustainable agriculture.

pages.title: What is an energy sustainability project?
pages.body:
An energy sustainability project is a planned effort to change the way a community, school or household uses energy — with the goal of reducing waste, switching to cleaner sources and making energy use more affordable and environmentally friendly in the long term.

> **DEFINITION** **Energy sustainability:** using energy in ways that meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own energy needs. **Energy efficiency:** producing the same amount of useful output (light, heat, movement) while using less energy, thereby reducing waste. **Energy audit:** a systematic survey of how energy is used in a place, identifying where it is wasted and how consumption can be reduced.

pages.body:
| **Project step** | **What to do** | **Example for a school project** |
|---|---|---|
| Step 1: Identify the problem | Survey your school or community to find out: what energy sources are used, how much energy is consumed, where energy is wasted and what the biggest energy costs are. | Walk through the school and note: all lights, fans and electronics; how many are left on unnecessarily; whether there are leaking pipes wasting pumped water; the monthly electricity bill. |
| Step 2: Research solutions | Find out what sustainable energy options are available, practical and affordable for your specific situation. Consider solar panels, biogas, LED lights, improved cookstoves, insulation and behaviour change. | Research the cost and output of solar panels suitable for powering school lights and computers. Find out if biogas could replace gas burners in the school canteen. |
| Step 3: Set clear goals | Define exactly what your project will achieve — specific, measurable targets. | Goal: Reduce the school's electricity bill by 20% within three months, AND install two solar-powered outdoor lights by the end of term. |
| Step 4: Plan the project | List the resources (money, materials, people, time) needed. Identify who will do each task and when. Anticipate challenges. | Budget: cost of LED bulbs, solar panel unit and installation. Responsibilities: students monitor energy use; school management funds equipment; local engineer installs panel. |
| Step 5: Carry out the project | Implement your plan: install equipment, change behaviour and monitor progress. | Replace all incandescent bulbs with LEDs. Run weekly checks that lights and fans are off when rooms are empty. Install the solar panel for outdoor lighting. |
| Step 6: Monitor and evaluate | After the project runs for some time, check whether it achieved its goals. Record the results and identify what worked and what needs improvement. | Compare electricity bills before and after. Measure whether outdoor areas are adequately lit. Survey students and teachers on whether they have changed their behaviour. |
| Step 7: Report and share | Present your findings to the school, community or district. Encourage others to replicate the project. | Present results at school assembly. Share the electricity savings achieved. Recommend the project to neighbouring schools. |

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Sustainable energy | Energy from sources that are naturally replenished and do not cause lasting environmental harm |
| Renewable energy | Energy from sources continuously replenished by nature, such as solar, wind and water |
| Non-renewable energy | Energy from finite sources that cannot be replaced once used, such as coal, oil and gas |
| Green economy | An economy that achieves growth while reducing pollution, emissions and environmental damage |
| Greenhouse effect | The process by which greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, warming the Earth |
| Greenhouse gases | Gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) that absorb infrared radiation and trap heat in the atmosphere |
| Global warming | The long-term rise in average Earth surface temperature due to the enhanced greenhouse effect |
| Climate change | Long-term shifts in global weather patterns and temperatures caused by global warming |
| Paris Agreement | An international treaty in which countries commit to reduce greenhouse gas emissions |
| Energy sustainability | Using energy to meet present needs without compromising future generations' ability to do the same |
| Energy efficiency | Producing the same useful output while using less energy |
| Energy audit | A systematic survey of energy use to identify waste and opportunities for improvement |
| Biogas | Methane gas produced by anaerobic decomposition of organic waste, used as cooking fuel |
| Reforestation | Planting trees to restore forests and help absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere |
| LED | Light-Emitting Diode: an energy-efficient light source using up to 80% less electricity than incandescent bulbs |
